title: 16. How the markets are intertwined
heading: How the markets are intertwined
label: Market linkages
summary: A map of which price moves which, across Taiwan, Korea, the Netherlands, Japan, the United States, and China; the firms that sit on each link; and the order in which shocks travel through the chain.

spans.text: The earlier chapters treat each market on its own. This one is about the wiring between them. The AI hardware economy is unusual in that a single product, the accelerator system, draws on the most concentrated suppliers in half a dozen countries at once, is financed in a seventh, and is consumed as tokens everywhere. A shock anywhere on the chain shows up as a price somewhere else, usually with a lag and usually in a different unit. The dashboard's linkage map draws this graph; this chapter is its legend.

spans.text: Two structural facts follow. The physical chain runs east to west (Netherlands and Japan supply Taiwan and Korea, which supply the United States) while the money runs west to east (US capital pays for Taiwanese and Korean capacity). And the token market at the top of the chain has become, through open weights, substantially Chinese in its model builders and its price-setting providers, while the routers and harnesses are largely American. A tariff, a control, or a currency move therefore hits different layers of the same product in different directions.
The heart of the chapter. Each row is an edge on the dashboard's linkage map. "Lag" is an order of magnitude, not a measurement.

spans.text: Because the chain has lead times, shocks arrive in a characteristic order, and knowing the order lets you tell a supply story from a demand story.

(a new model that earns much more per MW) shows up first in lab contract announcements and hyperscaler CapEx guidance, then in TSMC monthly revenue and ASML orders, then in HBM commentary, then, a year or more later, in delivered MW, and only then in rental indices, which fall as the capacity lands. The token price falls last.

(a packaging outage, an export control, a transformer shortage) shows up first in lead times and allocation notices, then in the rental index, which rises as marginal capacity tightens, then in token prices for the affected capability class, and finally in the financing layer, as projects that assumed delivery dates renegotiate.

(spreads widen, term premium rises) enters in the middle. It does not change today's physical supply, but it changes which planned supply gets built, so its first visible effect is on announcements and cancellations, and its physical effect arrives a year later as a supply shock.

The practical rule is that the same movement in a rental index means opposite things depending on what moved before it. A falling H100 rate after a year of rising TSMC revenue is capacity landing; a falling rate after a quarter of widening spreads is demand retreating.

blocks.text: 16.4 Where the graph is dense and where it is thin

spans.text: The linkage map is dense in the middle of the chain (foundry, memory, packaging, systems) because those layers are complementary: an accelerator needs all of them, so a shortage in one reprices the rest. It is thin at the ends. At the bottom, lithography has one supplier and no price, so ASML enters the graph as quantities and lead times. At the top, the token market has dozens of suppliers and very public prices, but, as
shows, prices that can be false; it enters the graph as a spread rather than a level.

For a Hayekian reader the density is the point. Where the graph is dense, prices in one market tell you about scarcity in another, which is the knowledge-communicating function working as designed. Where it is thin, either there is no price to carry the signal (HBM contracts) or the price is not trusted to carry it (cached tokens). The observatory's job is to draw the dense part faithfully and mark the thin part honestly.

The map on the dashboard is a graph, not a diagram. Nodes are markets and the firms that sit on them, colored by country. Edges are rows of the transmission table. Hovering a node lights up everything one step away; clicking opens the chapter that explains the edge. The map is drawn from this chapter's tables, so it changes when the tables do, and it makes no claim about correlation strength: the edge says that a mechanism exists, not that the mechanism was active last quarter. Correlation is what the cross-market chart beneath it is for, and that chart, like everything on the dashboard, is illustrative until source adapters replace it.
